item.title: How to Improve Your Well-Being by Agreeing to Disagree
item.description:
Agreeableness

How to Improve Your Well-Being by Agreeing to Disagree

Finding common ground can save you time, energy, and a headache.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • If more people listened and agreed with the speaker's undisputed facts, conversations could be more positive.
  • Practice the three "A's": agree, augment, and add.
  • Overall health can be improved by positive conversations, even when you disagree with the speaker.

For those true crime fans, or those simply following current trials in the national news, you have no doubt heard about accused murderer Lindsay Clancy. The parties do not dispute that Clancy killed her three young children: 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson, and 8-month-old Callan. Prosecutors contend the killings were planned and intentional. Her defense argues that she was not criminally responsible because she suffered a psychotic break.

Stipulation of Facts Agreed to by Prosecution and Defense

While the decision as to murder or insanity will be in the hands of a jury of 12, the prosecution and defense have reached certain stipulations: specific facts to which both parties agree. This avoids the necessity of numerous witnesses and lengthy testimony. For example, the parties agreed to chain of custody regarding biological samples, DNA, and some physical evidence, meaning that the parties agree the items were handled properly according to protocol. Good on them. Legally, given both parties agree she did kill the children, why not agree to those facts which are not disputed?

Shouldn't we all stipulate to agreed-to facts?

If only people approached real life with stipulations. Why can’t people at least agree to those facts which are not disputed? And why should they?

Agreeing to Disagree Is a Good Thing

Many have written about why and how “agreeing to disagree” can be a positive thing. Note how when someone starts to talk politics at a party, the temperature in the room immediately goes up. It isn’t necessarily that politics are divisive; it may be that people immediately react negatively, creating a negative, toxic environment around the discussion of politics.

Use the Triple-A Strategy to Disagree Agreeably

Agree: Instead, start with the facts you can agree with—stipulate, if you will. This is part of the “triple-A strategy” described to disagree agreeably. Agree, augment, and add. Listen and reply with “yes, I agree…”

It can be as simple as, “Yes, I agree it is difficult to discuss the political candidates for our district…” There is some aspect of what was said that you do actually agree with factually, so reach with agreement or appreciation.

Augment: To augment, pick up on a specific word or point and elaborate on what you agree with about it. “They both have extreme positions about…” This acts as a bridge between you and the speaker that you are both on the same page about the issues raised by the speaker; that you understand their point.

Add: Then add your point. Make your statement. Argue your position. Be careful though. Don’t use “but,” which has a negative effect. “I am stipulating to the photograph of the murder weapon, but I think it looks bigger than it is.” Instead, “I am stipulating to the photograph of the murder weapon, and note the ruler in the photograph demonstrates the actual size.”

A Positive Conversation Can Improve Well-Being

Here is why I stand by seeing what facts you can agree with to start, and then converse from there. Because it makes the exchange less emotional. You start in a common place and can then have a more positive conversation. And a more positive conversation can have positive health effects. Conversations with each other affect the quality of social relationships, which in large part determines a person’s well-being.

Listening and Agreeing Can Be a Good Thing

Agreeing to specific facts as a starting point in any conversation can lead to a real, listening dialogue and exchange. It diminishes the immediate knee-jerk defensive, negative emotions, which can lead to a positive experience, adding to a person’s overall health.

item.title: Choosing Who We Want to Be With One Another
item.description:
Relationships

Choosing Who We Want to Be With One Another

Four questions that bring greater intention and joy to our relationships.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • Our automatic reactions often protect us but may also repeat painful relationship patterns.
  • Difficult moments reveal who we choose to be with one another.
  • Remembering what truly matters can shift conflict from winning toward connection.
  • Entering with an intention, rather than a script, creates room for understanding, flexibility, and joy.
Source: Image by Author with ChatGPT

Relationships are not shaped only by the love we feel. They are also shaped by the way we respond when love becomes difficult, when we feel hurt, criticized, rejected, disappointed, or misunderstood.

In these emotionally charged moments, our nervous system often reacts before our wiser self has time to respond. We may attack, defend, withdraw, blame, explain, or attempt to prove that we are right. These reactions are deeply human. They are often protective strategies that we developed long before the present conversation began.

Yet, when we repeatedly enter a relationship from the same familiar emotional place, we are likely to create the same familiar outcome. The relationship path invites us to do something different. It is a path that moves, step by step, from automatic reaction toward awareness, intention, compassion, and conscious choice.

Four Questions That Can Guide the Relationship Path

1. What Kind of World Do I Want to Live In and Help Create?

This may sound like a philosophical question, yet it is also deeply practical. The world we wish to inhabit begins with the emotional world we create between ourselves and another person.

Do I want to help create a world dominated by judgment, defensiveness, fear, and competition, or one that includes greater respect, honesty, compassion, responsibility, and care? We do not create this world only through major decisions. We create it through our tone of voice, the words we choose, the assumptions we make, and the way we respond when someone disappoints us.

If I want to live in a kinder and more compassionate world, I must ask how I can contribute to creating that world in my relationships.

2. Who Do I Want to Be in That World?

It is relatively easy to be kind and generous when we feel safe, appreciated, and loved. The deeper challenge is deciding who we want to be when we feel hurt, threatened, dismissed, or misunderstood.

Perhaps I want to be courageous without becoming aggressive, honest without becoming cruel, and compassionate without abandoning myself. Conscious choice does not mean suppressing anger or pretending that everything is fine. It means developing enough awareness to allow our emotions to inform us without permitting them to control our behavior.

I cannot always choose what I feel, but I can practice choosing how I relate to what I feel and how I express it.

3. What Truly Matters to Me in This Relationship?

During conflict, it is easy to lose sight of what matters most. We may become so determined to win the argument that we damage the connection. We may demand to be understood while making it nearly impossible for the other person to feel understood. We may protect ourselves from vulnerability while simultaneously longing for greater intimacy.

This question asks us to look beyond the immediate disagreement. What truly matters to me: trust, honesty, closeness, mutual respect, emotional safety, partnership, growth, or playfulness?

Knowing what matters does not eliminate conflict, nor does it require us to surrender our position. Rather, it gives the conflict direction. It reminds us that the person in front of us is not simply an opponent in an argument, but someone with whom we are trying to build something meaningful.

4. What Would I Like to Happen in the Next Conversation?

Before answering this question, it is important to pause because our automatic mind will quickly translate it into something familiar: “I want him to understand me,” “I want her to admit that she was wrong,” “I want us to agree,” or “I want this conversation to end differently.”

These wishes are understandable, but notice that they depend primarily on what we want the other person to do.

The deeper question is not, “What would I like my partner to do?” but rather, “What would I like to happen between us?” The difference is significant because it shifts our attention from controlling another person toward creating a relational experience.

Perhaps I would like us to listen more deeply, feel safer, and bring greater curiosity, honesty, gentleness, and understanding into the conversation. This does not mean that we must agree. It means that I want the way we meet each other to be different.

Once I identify what I would like to happen between us, another question naturally follows: What do I want to bring into this conversation to increase the possibility that it will happen?

Bringing Compassion Into the Conversation

Compassion does not mean excusing hurtful behavior, avoiding accountability, or giving up our boundaries. It means recognizing the humanity beneath the behavior, including the fear, pain, longing, or vulnerability that may be driving it. It also means extending that same understanding toward ourselves.

When I notice myself becoming defensive, I can acknowledge that a part of me is trying to protect myself. Rather than judging or suppressing that reaction, I can listen to it, regulate myself, and then decide whether my automatic response represents the person I want to be.

I cannot guarantee how the other person will respond, but I can take responsibility for the emotional qualities I bring into the interaction.

Showing Up With Joy

Joy may appear to be an unusual quality to bring into a difficult conversation, but relational joy does not mean denying pain, forcing positivity, or pretending that a serious issue is unimportant. It is the warmth, gratitude, and aliveness we bring to the connection, even while addressing something painful.

Joy may be expressed through tenderness in our voice, gentle humor, affectionate touch when appropriate, or a simple acknowledgment: “This is difficult, but I am grateful that we are willing to talk about it.”

Joy reminds us that relationships are not merely problems to solve. They are also places where we can experience affection, playfulness, discovery, growth, and shared meaning. Even during conflict, we can remember that the person in front of us is more than the behavior that frustrates us. This is someone with whom we have shared experiences, struggles, dreams, and perhaps deep love.

Entering With a Script or an Intention

There is a profound difference between entering a conversation with a script and entering it with an intention. When I arrive with a script, I have already decided how the conversation should unfold, what the other person should say, and how it should end. It is like a fulfilling prophecy.

When I arrive with an intention, I know how I want to show up, to the best of my ability. Intention allows me to remain flexible, creative, compassionate, and grounded, regardless of how the other person responds.

A script seeks to control the outcome. An intention helps me remain faithful to the path and to the person I have chosen to become.

An Invitation to Practice

Before your next important conversation, ask yourself what you would like to happen between you and what you want to bring into the interaction to increase the possibility that it can happen. Consider how you might offer greater compassion to yourself and the other person, and how you might introduce a little more warmth, gratitude, or joy.

Do not rush to find the perfect answers. Carry the questions with you and let them shape how you enter the conversation.

Remember, intention does not guarantee the outcome. It chooses the path you aspire to create.
